VIEWS, WITH WHO HOLDS THEM · THIS PAGE
Is Simon the Zealot the same man as Simon the Lord's brother, or Symeon son of Clopas? (Earliest source first.)
Hegesippus (about AD 170) and Eusebius (about AD 325), who never call Symeon an apostle; A. C. McGiffert (1890)

Hegesippus tells of Symeon son of Clopas, second bishop of Jerusalem, martyred under Trajan “at the age of one hundred and twenty years”; Eusebius, retelling it, says he “suffered a death similar to that of our Lord”, and calls him “a cousin, as they say, of the Saviour”. Neither calls him one of the Twelve. McGiffert holds that the Lord's brothers were not apostles, since they did not believe in him.
Early church John 7:5 Eusebius (trans. A. C. McGiffert, 1890·A. C. McGiffert, 1890
Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend (about 1260); noted by C. M. Kerr (ISBE, 1915)
The Golden Legend makes Simon and Jude brothers of James the Less and sons of “Mary Cleophas”; Kerr notes that Simon “has been identified with Simon the brother of Jesus”.
Later tradition Mark 6:3 Jacobus de Voragine (Caxton's English of 1483, 1900·C. M. Kerr, 1915
C. M. Kerr (ISBE, 1915), drawing on Ethiopic texts translated by Budge
Kerr argues that Simon may be Nathanael, citing an Ethiopic “Preaching of Simon, son of Cleopas”, whose heading calls him “Judas, which is interpreted Nathanael”.
